title: Other income
summary: Article 21 is the residual rule for income that no other Article covers. The OECD Model gives the residence State the sole right to tax it, wherever it arises, unless the income is connected with a PE in the other State.
readingNote: Many Saudi treaties add a UN-style paragraph that lets the State where the income arises also tax it. Where the Saudi wording has such a paragraph, the OECD guidance on exclusive residence taxation (paragraphs 2 and 3 below) does not apply to that income. Check the treaty text alongside this tab.

entries.t: The Article covers income of a class not dealt with elsewhere, and income from sources not mentioned elsewhere, including income from third States. For example, it stops the other Contracting State taxing third-State income of a dual resident whom Article 4 treats as resident only in the first State.
The residence State gets the exclusive right to tax. Where both States claim residence, Article 4 decides, including for third-State income.

The rule applies even if the residence State does not actually tax the income. The other State cannot tax income arising there, or third-State income of a person Article 4 treats as resident elsewhere. To avoid non-taxation, States may agree to make the rule conditional on taxation in the residence State.

sections.heading: Paragraph 2: income connected with a PE

entries.t: Income connected with a PE that a resident has in the other State, including third-State income, may be taxed by the PE State. This does not apply to immovable property, which the State where it is situated taxes first under Article 6(4).

It also covers cases where payer and recipient are residents of the same State but the income is attributable to the recipient's PE in the other State. The residence State then gives relief under Article 23.

A right or property is effectively connected with the PE if its 'economic' ownership is allocated to the PE under the OECD report on attributing profits to PEs. Insurance PEs follow Part IV of the report, applied flexibly.

Attaching shares, bonds or patents to a PE in an exemption-method State to get better treatment is countered by Article 29(9). Recording assets in a PE's books is not enough to make them effectively connected.

sections.heading: Optional paragraph on excessive amounts between related parties

entries.t: States that have had difficulty with non-traditional financial instruments between related parties can add a paragraph limiting the Article to the arm's length amount, as Article 11(6) does for interest.
The same principles as Article 11 apply. It is not meant for alimony or social security, but for instruments that would not have been entered into without the special relationship.

Unlike Article 11, all payments under such an instrument may be treated as excessive. Because no other distributive Article applies to Article 21 income, the excess is taxable under each State's domestic law. Articles 23, 25 and 26 still apply to it.

membersNote: Paragraphs 13 to 19 are members' reservations on the Article. Non-OECD economies' positions are in section P(21): many of them keep the right to tax other income arising in their territory. Those relevant to your treaty appear in the Other countries tab.

source.title: OECD (2026), Model Tax Convention on Income and on Capital 2025 (Full Version)
